q: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
note: The Sahara covers roughly the same area as the entire United States.

q: Which mountain is the highest point on Earth above sea level?
note: Its summit sits directly on the border between Nepal and China.

q: Which is the largest island in the world?
note: Australia is bigger, but geographers class it as a continental landmass rather than an island.

q: On which continent is the Atacama Desert?
note: Some weather stations in the Atacama have gone decades without recording measurable rain.

q: Which volcano buried the Roman city of Pompeii in AD 79?
note: The same eruption buried nearby Herculaneum, preserving both towns under ash for centuries.

q: Which peninsula do Spain and Portugal share?
note: Andorra and Gibraltar sit on the same peninsula, tucked into its edges.

q: Which mountain range is traditionally taken as the dividing line between Europe and Asia in Russia?
note: The Urals run roughly north to south for about 1,500 miles, from the Arctic coast to Kazakhstan.

q: Name the highest mountain in Africa.
note: Kilimanjaro is a dormant volcano in Tanzania that rises alone from the plain rather than as part of a range.

q: Which mountain range runs down the entire western edge of South America?
note: At roughly 4,300 miles, the Andes form the longest continental mountain range on Earth.

q: Which volcano erupted catastrophically in Washington State in May 1980?
note: The blast took roughly 1,300 feet off the top of the mountain and left a horseshoe-shaped crater.

q: Which desert stretches across southern Mongolia and northern China?
note: Unlike the Sahara, the Gobi is a cold desert where winter temperatures drop far below freezing.

q: On which Italian island would you find Mount Etna?
note: Etna is the most active volcano in Europe and has been erupting on and off for thousands of years.

q: Which mountain is the second highest in the world?
note: K2 straddles the China-Pakistan border and has a far higher climbing death rate than Everest.

q: Which island nation off the southeast coast of Africa is the world's fourth largest island?
note: Madagascar split from the African mainland so long ago that most of its wildlife exists nowhere else.

q: The Yucatan Peninsula lies mostly within which country?
note: The peninsula is honeycombed with cenotes, sinkholes that open into flooded limestone caves.

q: Which mountain is the highest peak in North America?
a: Denali, also known as Mount McKinley
note: The Alaskan peak rises to about 20,300 feet, and its older name means roughly "the tall one" in Koyukon.

q: What is the highest mountain in the contiguous 48 United States?
note: Whitney's summit in California stands less than 100 miles from Badwater Basin, the lowest point in North America.

q: Name the peninsula that makes up mainland Denmark and reaches into northern Germany.
note: Denmark's capital, Copenhagen, is not on Jutland at all but across the water on the island of Zealand.

q: Which coastal desert in southwestern Africa gives its name to a country?
note: Fog drifting in off the cold Atlantic is the main source of moisture for life in the Namib.

q: What is the largest peninsula in the world?
note: Saudi Arabia takes up the bulk of it, with Yemen and Oman along the southern rim.

q: What is the capital of Canada?
note: Queen Victoria settled on Ottawa in 1857 as a compromise between rival cities including Toronto and Quebec City.

q: What is the capital of Australia?
note: Canberra was built from scratch as a compromise capital because Sydney and Melbourne could not agree.

q: Which is the largest country in the world by land area?
note: Russia is so wide that it shares a land border with Norway in the northwest and North Korea in the far east.

q: Cairo is the capital of which country?
note: Cairo sits at the head of the Nile Delta, where the river fans out toward the Mediterranean.

q: Stockholm is the capital of which Scandinavian country?
note: Stockholm is spread across more than a dozen islands where a large lake drains into the Baltic Sea.

q: What is the capital of Japan?
note: The city was called Edo until 1868, when the emperor moved there and it was renamed Tokyo, or "eastern capital."

q: What is the capital of Brazil?
note: Brasilia was purpose-built in the empty interior and took over as capital from Rio de Janeiro in 1960.

q: What is the capital of Turkey?
note: Ankara replaced Istanbul as the capital in 1923, when the Turkish republic was founded.

q: Which tiny country sits high in the Pyrenees between France and Spain?
note: Andorra has been governed since 1278 by two co-princes: the French head of state and a Spanish bishop.

q: What is the capital of New Zealand?
note: Wellington is the southernmost capital city of any sovereign country.

q: Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
note: Lesotho is one of only three countries in the world entirely enclosed by a single other country.

q: What is the capital of Morocco?
note: Casablanca and Marrakesh are better known abroad, but the government sits in Rabat on the Atlantic coast.

q: Which South American country takes its name from the Spanish word for the equator?
note: The equator itself passes just north of the capital, Quito.

q: Which South American country has two capitals, La Paz and Sucre?
note: Sucre is the constitutional capital, while the government does its business up in La Paz.

q: Which is the smallest sovereign country in the world by area?
note: The whole country covers about 110 acres, tucked inside the city of Rome.

q: What is the capital of Switzerland?
note: Zurich and Geneva are larger and more famous, but Bern has held the federal government since 1848.

q: Which African country was settled by freed American slaves and declared independence in 1847?
note: Its capital, Monrovia, is named after US President James Monroe.

q: Ljubljana is the capital of which European country?
note: Slovenia broke away from Yugoslavia in 1991 after a conflict that lasted only ten days.

q: Which is the only country with coastline on both the Caspian Sea and the Persian Gulf?
note: Iran was known internationally as Persia until it asked the world to use its own name in 1935.

q: Which country governs the western half of the island of New Guinea?
note: The eastern half is the separate country of Papua New Guinea, and the border is a nearly straight line.

q: Which US state is the largest by area?
note: Alaska is more than twice the size of Texas, the runner-up.

q: In which US state is the Grand Canyon?
note: The canyon runs for about 277 river miles and in places is a mile deep.

q: Which US state is made up entirely of islands?
note: Hawaii joined the Union in 1959 as the fiftieth state, a few months after Alaska.

q: Which American city is nicknamed the Windy City?
note: The nickname is often traced to the city's boastful politicians rather than to the weather off Lake Michigan.

q: Which US state is nicknamed the Lone Star State?
note: The single star recalls the years Texas spent as an independent republic before joining the Union in 1845.

q: Which US state is known as the Golden State?
note: Gold was found at Sutter's Mill in 1848, and California became a state just two years later.

q: Yellowstone National Park lies mostly within which US state?
note: Narrow strips of the park spill over into Montana and Idaho.

q: Which US state is nicknamed the Show-Me State?
note: The phrase is usually traced to an 1899 speech by a Missouri congressman boasting of his state's skepticism.

q: What is the capital of New York State?
note: Albany has held the job since 1797 and is one of the oldest continuously chartered cities in the country.

q: Which US state shares a land border with only one other state?
note: Maine touches only New Hampshire, and beyond that its neighbor is Canada.

q: Which American city sits where the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers meet?
note: The two rivers join at that spot to form the Ohio River.

q: Which US state is the smallest by area?
note: You could fit more than 400 Rhode Islands inside Alaska.

q: What name is given to the only spot in the United States where four states meet at a single point?
note: Arizona, Utah, Colorado and New Mexico all touch there.

q: Bourbon Street runs through the French Quarter of which American city?
note: The street is named for the French royal House of Bourbon, not for the whiskey.

q: Which mountain range runs through the eastern United States from Georgia up to Maine?
note: The Appalachian Trail follows them for roughly 2,200 miles.

q: Which is the only US state named after a US president?
note: The nation's capital carries his name too, but the District of Columbia is not a state.

q: What is the capital of Vermont?
note: The town takes its name from Montpellier in southern France.

q: Which US state capital sits at the highest elevation?
note: Santa Fe stands about 7,000 feet up in the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo mountains.

q: Which city, founded by the Spanish in 1565, is the oldest continuously occupied European settlement in the continental United States?
note: Spanish settlers were living there more than forty years before the English founded Jamestown.

q: Which US state contains the geographic center of the contiguous 48 states?
note: A stone marker near the small town of Lebanon, Kansas claims the spot.

q: Which is the largest of the world's oceans?
note: The Pacific covers more of the globe than all the world's dry land put together.

q: Which river flows the length of Egypt and empties into the Mediterranean?
note: Ancient Egypt depended on the Nile's yearly flood, which the Aswan High Dam has held back since the 1960s.

q: Which river runs through Paris?
note: The Seine empties into the English Channel at the port of Le Havre.

q: Which is the largest of the five Great Lakes?
note: Superior holds more water than the other four Great Lakes combined.

q: Which river forms the border between Texas and Mexico?
note: On the Mexican side the same river is called the Rio Bravo.

q: Which river flows through London?
note: The Thames is tidal through London and runs east into the North Sea.

q: Which is the largest lake in the world by surface area?
note: Despite the name it is a landlocked lake, bordered by Russia, Iran, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan.

q: The Strait of Gibraltar connects the Atlantic Ocean to which sea?
note: The strait is only about eight miles across at its narrowest point.

q: Which river flows through Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade?
note: The Danube touches ten countries on its way to the Black Sea, more than any other river.

q: Which lake, bordered by Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya, is the largest in Africa?
note: The White Nile begins at its northern shore in Uganda.

q: Which is the deepest lake in the world?
note: This Siberian lake holds roughly a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh surface water on Earth.

q: Which sacred Indian river flows past Varanasi and empties into the Bay of Bengal?
note: The Ganges begins as meltwater in the Himalayas before crossing the plains of northern India.

q: Which body of water between Israel and Jordan sits at the lowest land elevation on Earth?
note: Its shore lies more than 1,300 feet below sea level, and the water is salty enough to float a swimmer.

q: Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
note: It is the only ocean named after a country.

q: Which major river flows north through Germany and the Netherlands into the North Sea?
note: The Rhine marked the frontier of the Roman Empire and has been a trade artery ever since.

q: What is the name of the deepest known trench in the world's oceans?
note: Its deepest point, the Challenger Deep, lies nearly 36,000 feet down in the western Pacific near Guam.

q: Which sea has no coastline at all, its edges defined instead by ocean currents?
note: It sits in the North Atlantic, ringed by four currents, and is named for the sargassum seaweed that drifts there.

q: Which is the longest river in Asia?
note: The Three Gorges Dam spans it, and the river runs entirely within China.

q: Which is the longest river in Europe?
note: The Volga flows entirely inside Russia and drains into the Caspian Sea rather than any ocean.

q: Which African lake is the longest freshwater lake in the world?
note: It stretches roughly 400 miles along the Great Rift Valley and is the second deepest lake on Earth.

q: In which city would you find the Colosseum?
note: The arena was built to hold an estimated 50,000 spectators for gladiator games and staged hunts.

q: In which country is the Taj Mahal?
note: It was built in the 1600s as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal, wife of the emperor Shah Jahan.

q: The Statue of Liberty was a gift to the United States from which country?
note: It was dedicated in 1886, and its iron framework was engineered by Gustave Eiffel.

q: In which American city is Times Square?
note: The square was renamed in 1904 for The New York Times, which had just moved its offices there.

q: The famous Leaning Tower stands in which Italian city?
note: The bell tower started tilting while it was still being built in the 1170s, because the ground beneath it was too soft.

q: In which city is the Forbidden City?
note: The palace complex housed Chinese emperors for nearly 500 years, until 1912.

q: In which country are the ruins of Machu Picchu?
note: The Inca site perches about 8,000 feet up on a ridge above the Urubamba valley.

q: In which city does the Brandenburg Gate stand?
note: From 1961 to 1989 the gate sat stranded in the no-man's-land beside the Berlin Wall.

q: In which city is the Kremlin?
note: The word kremlin simply means fortress in Russian, and other Russian cities have their own.

q: Which city is home to both the Blue Mosque and the Hagia Sophia?
note: Istanbul spreads across both Europe and Asia, divided by the Bosporus strait.

q: In which country is the ancient city of Petra, carved into rose-colored rock?
note: Petra was the capital of the Nabataean traders more than two thousand years ago.

q: The statue of Christ the Redeemer looks out over which city?
note: The statue stands on Corcovado mountain, some 2,300 feet above the harbor.

q: The Golden Gate Bridge spans the entrance to which bay?
note: Its paint color has an official name: International Orange.

q: In which city would you climb the Acropolis to reach the Parthenon?
note: The Parthenon went up in the fifth century BC as a temple to the goddess Athena.

q: In which country is Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world?
note: Built in the 12th century as a Hindu temple, it was later converted to Buddhist use and never abandoned.

q: Which European city is built across more than a hundred small islands in a lagoon?
note: Its buildings rest on millions of wooden piles driven down into the mud of the lagoon floor.

q: In which country is the fabled desert city of Timbuktu?
note: Timbuktu grew rich on the trans-Saharan trade and became a famed center of Islamic scholarship.

q: The Alhambra palace complex overlooks which Spanish city?
note: The Alhambra was the seat of the last Muslim rulers in Spain, who surrendered it in 1492.

q: The Winter Palace and the Hermitage Museum are in which Russian city?
note: Peter the Great founded the city on marshland in 1703, and it was called Leningrad from 1924 to 1991.

q: The buried Terracotta Army was discovered near which Chinese city?
note: Farmers digging a well in 1974 struck the first of thousands of life-size clay soldiers.

q: Which country's flag features a single red maple leaf?
note: The maple leaf flag was adopted in 1965, replacing a design based on the British Red Ensign.

q: Which country flies a flag showing a plain red circle on a white field?
note: The Japanese call it the Hinomaru, meaning circle of the sun.

q: How many time zones does the contiguous United States span?
note: Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific, with Alaska and Hawaii adding two more beyond them.

q: What is the name of the imaginary line at zero degrees latitude?
note: It crosses through Ecuador, Kenya, Indonesia and Brazil, among other countries.

q: What is the name of the line of zero degrees longitude that runs through Greenwich, England?
note: An international conference fixed it at Greenwich in 1884, beating out rival lines through Paris and elsewhere.

q: What is the name of the line running roughly down the middle of the Pacific where the calendar date changes?
note: It zigzags rather than running straight, so island groups can keep the same day as their neighbors.

q: Which is the only country whose national flag is not a rectangle or a square?
note: Nepal's flag is two stacked triangular pennants, a shape carried over from much older banners.

q: Which country flies a square flag bearing a white cross on red?
note: Switzerland and Vatican City are the only two countries whose flags are square.

q: Which South American country borders more other countries than any other on the continent?
note: Brazil touches every country in South America except Chile and Ecuador.

q: What is the name of the line of latitude marking the northern edge of the tropics?
note: It marks the farthest north the sun can ever stand directly overhead, which happens around June 21.

q: Which country lies south of North Korea, across a border first drawn along the 38th parallel?
note: The two were split along that line in 1945, and the demilitarized zone still runs near it.

q: Which country's flag shows a blue Star of David between two blue horizontal stripes?
note: The stripes echo the bands on a traditional Jewish prayer shawl.

q: What is the name of the narrow strip of land that joins North and South America?
note: The Panama Canal cuts straight through it, saving ships the long trip around South America.

q: Which continent has no permanent human residents?
note: Antarctica also counts as the world's largest desert, since almost no precipitation falls there.

q: Besides Vatican City, which other tiny republic is entirely surrounded by Italy?
note: San Marino claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic, traditionally dated to AD 301.

q: Which Himalayan kingdom flies a flag featuring a white dragon?
note: Bhutan calls itself Druk Yul, which means Land of the Thunder Dragon.

q: Which African country is surrounded by Senegal on every side except its short Atlantic coast?
note: The country is essentially a narrow ribbon of land following the banks of the river it is named for.

q: Which US state contains the Northwest Angle, the only part of the lower 48 states lying north of the 49th parallel?
note: The Angle is cut off from the rest of the state by water, so driving there means passing through Canada.

q: Which is the only US state whose name begins with two vowels?
note: Ohio, Oregon, Oklahoma and Utah all start with a vowel, but each follows it with a consonant.

q: Which Pacific island nation lies in all four hemispheres at once?
note: Its islands straddle both the equator and the 180th meridian, and in 1995 it shifted the date line east so the whole country shares one day.
